lead: One transistor forces a trade. A common-emitter (CE) stage gives voltage gain, but its Miller capacitance limits bandwidth. An emitter follower gives high input resistance, but only one transistor's β. Two-transistor pairs remove both weaknesses. A common-base (CB) stage stacked on a CE stage shields the lower collector capacitance: the cascode, a wideband gain stage. Two emitter followers stacked multiply current gain: the Darlington pair, a high-resistance buffer. Both appear inside op-amps, regulators and power drivers.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.5 for CE, CB and CC gains, and Chapter 2.7 for direct coupling.

sections.h3: The cascode: a common-emitter feeding a common-base

blocks.text: A CE amplifier loses high-frequency gain because of the base-collector capacitance C<sub>bc</sub>, a few picofarads. Base and collector swing in antiphase, so the voltage across C<sub>bc</sub> is (1 + |A<sub>v</sub>|) times the input. The input then sees Miller capacitance C<sub>M</sub> = C<sub>bc</sub>(1 + g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>L</sub>). Here g<sub>m</sub> is transconductance in siemens (A/V), and R<sub>L</sub> is the collector load in ohms. With source resistance R<sub>s</sub>, this gives a pole at f = 1/(2πR<sub>s</sub>C<sub>M</sub>), which sets bandwidth. Remove the collector swing and you remove the problem.

The cascode uses a second transistor. Q1 is a CE stage. Its collector drives the emitter of Q2, whose base is held at fixed DC voltage, so Q2 works as a CB stage. The load R<sub>L</sub> is at Q2's collector. Q1's signal current i<sub>c1</sub> = g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>be1</sub> flows into Q2's emitter and out of its collector almost unchanged, because α ≈ 1.

blocks.where: g<sub>m1</sub> is Q1's transconductance in A/V, R<sub>L</sub> is the load at Q2's collector in ohms, and the minus sign means the output is inverted.

blocks.text: Q1's collector looks into Q2's emitter, a low-resistance node of about 1/g<sub>m2</sub>, roughly 25 Ω at 1 mA. So Q1's collector swings by only v<sub>o1</sub> ≈ −g<sub>m1</sub>v<sub>be1</sub>/g<sub>m2</sub> ≈ −v<sub>be1</sub>. The Miller factor falls from (1 + g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>L</sub>) to about 2. Input capacitance falls from hundreds of picofarads to a few, and the input pole moves out by about the gain ratio.

The price is headroom: about 1 V extra between supply and output. The reward is very high output resistance. Looking into Q2's collector, R<sub>out</sub> ≈ g<sub>m2</sub>r<sub>o2</sub>r<sub>o1</sub> ≈ β<sub>2</sub>r<sub>o2</sub>. That is poor for driving a load and excellent for a current source, which is why folded-cascode op-amps use it.

sections.h3: The Darlington pair: two emitter followers

blocks.text: An emitter follower has R<sub>in</sub> ≈ βR<sub>E</sub>. When that is not enough, feed Q1's emitter into Q2's base. Both collectors go to V<sub>CC</sub>; the signal enters Q1's base and leaves Q2's emitter. This is two common-collector stages in direct cascade: a Darlington pair.

blocks.where: β<sub>D</sub> is the current gain of the pair, β1 of Q1, and β2 of Q2.

blocks.text: Q1's emitter current is Q2's base current, I<sub>E1</sub> = I<sub>B2</sub>. So I<sub>E2</sub> = (β2 + 1)(β1 + 1)I<sub>B1</sub>. A base current of 10 µA can control 100 mA. For small signals the pair acts as one transistor with current gain β<sub>D</sub>, input resistance R<sub>in</sub> ≈ β<sub>D</sub>R<sub>E</sub>, and V<sub>BE(total)</sub> = V<sub>BE1</sub> + V<sub>BE2</sub> ≈ 1.4 V.

Q1 never saturates. Its collector-emitter voltage is only V<sub>CE1</sub> = V<sub>BE2</sub> ≈ 0.7 V, above V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> ≈ 0.2 V. The pair saturates at about V<sub>BE2</sub> + V<sub>CE2(sat)</sub> ≈ 0.9 V. The 1.4 V offset is the cost: on a 3.3 V supply it eats almost half the swing.

Uses: buffering a high-resistance sensor into a low-resistance load, voltmeter inputs, and driver ICs such as the ULN2003 switching relays and stepper windings. A complementary Darlington, some syllabi call it the Sziklai pair, uses one PNP and one NPN, gives the same β<sub>D</sub>, and needs only about 0.7 V offset.

head: Property
Cascode (CE + CB)
Darlington (CC + CC)
rows: r<sub>π</sub> of Q1, a few kΩ

blocks.text: The cascode keeps CE voltage gain and buys bandwidth; input resistance stays low because signal enters Q1's base. The Darlington buys input resistance and current gain; voltage gain stays about 1. A receiver front end can use both: a Darlington at the input, a cascode for gain.

Only a few universities teach cascode frequency analysis here. Pole positions and gain-bandwidth estimates belong to Unit 3. Unit 5 covers folded-cascode current sources and op-amp input stages built from these blocks.

figure.caption: Top chain: a CE stage feeds a CB stage; the upper device shields the lower collector capacitance, keeping gain high while widening bandwidth. Bottom chain: two emitter followers multiply current gains.

spec.title: Two compound pairs
spec.aria: Two signal chains from a common input: one through a common-emitter then common-base stage to a high-gain output, the other through two emitter followers to a high input-resistance output.

examples.question: A Darlington pair uses β1 = β2 = 100 and drives R<sub>E</sub> = 100 Ω. The emitter current is 100 mA and each base-emitter drop is 0.7 V. (a) Find β<sub>D</sub> and base current. (b) Find input resistance. (c) Find DC base voltage. (d) Compare with one β = 100 transistor driving the same R<sub>E</sub>.
steps: Single transistor: I<sub>B</sub> = 100 mA / 100 = 1 mA; R<sub>in</sub> ≈ 100 × 100 Ω = 10 kΩ.
The pair gives 100 times the input resistance for one hundredth the base current, costing 0.7 V extra headroom.
examples.answer: β<sub>D</sub> = 10,000, I<sub>B</sub> = 10 µA, R<sub>in</sub> = 1 MΩ, V<sub>B</sub> = 11.4 V; a single β = 100 transistor needs 1 mA and offers 10 kΩ.
examples.check:
beta1 = 100
beta2 = 100
RE = 100.0
IE = 100e-3
VBE = 0.7

beta_D = beta1 * beta2
IB = IE / beta_D
Rin = beta_D * RE
VB = 2 * VBE + IE * RE
IB_single = IE / beta1
Rin_single = beta1 * RE

print(beta_D)
print(IB * 1e6)
print(Rin)
print(VB)
print(IB_single * 1e3)
print(Rin_single)

traps: Writing β<sub>D</sub> = β1 + β2 instead of β1β2. Base currents add, emitter currents multiply.
Forgetting the Darlington's ≈ 1.4 V base-emitter drop. It eats headroom in a 3.3 V or 5 V supply and clips the output early.
Calling any two-transistor stack a cascode. The upper device must be common base; taking output from Q1's collector gives an ordinary CE stage with no bandwidth benefit.
Expecting the cascode to raise input resistance. It raises output resistance; input still sees r<sub>π</sub> of Q1.
Sign slip on cascode gain: A<sub>v</sub> ≈ −g<sub>m1</sub>R<sub>L</sub>. The stage inverts like the CE stage it replaces.

quiz.a: A CE stage whose collector drives the emitter of a CB stage, with output at the CB collector.

quiz.q: Write the Darlington current gain and total base-emitter voltage.
Why does the cascode reduce input Miller capacitance?
quiz.a: Q1's collector looks into Q2's emitter, about 1/g<sub>m2</sub>. Q1's collector swings by only about −v<sub>be</sub>, so C<sub>bc</sub> sees a factor near 2 instead of (1 + g<sub>m1</sub>R<sub>L</sub>).

quiz.q: Why does the input transistor of a Darlington pair stay out of saturation?
quiz.a: Its V<sub>CE</sub> equals Q2's V<sub>BE</sub> ≈ 0.7 V, above V<sub>CE(sat)</sub> ≈ 0.2 V, even when Q2 saturates.

quiz.q: A cascode has g<sub>m1</sub> = 40 mS and R<sub>L</sub> = 2 kΩ. Find voltage gain.
A Darlington has β1 = 50, β2 = 80, R<sub>E</sub> = 1 kΩ. Find β<sub>D</sub> and input resistance.
A 1 MΩ source must drive a 1 kΩ load at 5 MHz with gain 100. Which pair goes where?
quiz.a: Use a Darlington first: its input resistance is in the megaohm range and its output resistance is low. Then a cascode gives gain ≈ −g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>L</sub> with Miller capacitance shielded, keeping the input pole beyond 5 MHz. A plain CE gives gain but loses bandwidth; an emitter follower alone gives no voltage gain.

beyond: Not for the exam. Folded-cascode amplifiers dominate CMOS op-amps because they give high output resistance and wide bandwidth at low supply. Discrete Darlingtons now live mainly in driver ICs, but Sziklai and composite pairs remain in audio output stages and gate drives. RF low-noise amplifiers use the cascode to trade headroom for stability and bandwidth.
